pos: noun
Names a person, place, thing or idea.
Most nouns can follow the; names of people and places are nouns too.
scientist, Lagos, telescope, freedom
pronoun
Stands in for a noun the reader already knows.
Which, who and that are pronouns too when they open a clause that describes a noun.
it, they, them, she, someone
verb
Says what the subject does or is.
Only a tensed verb can be the verb of a clause: kept, is, has kept. An -ing, to or -ed form with no helping verb cannot: keeping, to keep, kept by.
discovered, is, has collected, will open
adjective
Describes a noun: which one, what kind, how many.
It usually sits right before its noun or after is: a rare coin, the coin is rare.
ancient, blue, rare, careful
adverb
Describes a verb, an adjective, another adverb or a whole clause: how, when, where, how much.
Transitions such as however and therefore are adverbs, not conjunctions, so a comma alone cannot join two sentences with them.
quickly, rarely, very, soon
preposition
A short word that ties a noun to the rest of the sentence, often to show place, time or connection.
A preposition and its noun make a prepositional phrase: in the lab, of the samples. The subject is never inside one: in The box of samples is heavy, the subject is box.
in, on, of, by, during, between, without
conjunction
Joins words, phrases or clauses.
Coordinating conjunctions (and, but, or, so, yet, for, nor) can join two sentences after a comma. Subordinating ones (because, although, when, while, if, since) make a clause that cannot stand alone.
and, but, because, although
determiner
Comes before a noun to point to it or count it.
The and a are the commonest. Possessives such as its and their are determiners too.
the, a, this, these, its, their, many
terms: Noun
A word that names a person, place, thing or idea: scientist, Lagos, freedom.
Noun phrase
A noun with the words that describe it: the oldest bridge in the city.
Pronoun
A word that stands in for a noun: it, they, someone.
Verb
A word that says what the subject does or is. See tensed verb.
Helping verb
A verb such as is, has, will or can that comes before another verb form: has kept, was found.
Adjective
A word that describes a noun: rare, ancient.
Adverb
A word that describes a verb, an adjective or a whole clause: quickly, very, however.
Preposition
A short word that ties a noun to the rest of the sentence: in, of, by, during.
Prepositional phrase
A preposition and the noun it ties in: in the lab, of the samples. The subject of a sentence is never inside one.
Subordinating conjunction
Because, although, when, while, if, since and the like: words that turn a clause into one that cannot stand alone.
Subject
The noun or pronoun a clause is about: who or what does the verb.

try.note: During the storm is a prepositional phrase. The subject is keeper and the tensed verb is lit.
But is a coordinating conjunction, so a comma before it can join two sentences: The scientists tested the samples and they found no trace of iron.
Because is a subordinating conjunction: Because the river rose quickly cannot stand alone, so it leans on the village moved its school.

cards.t: Because the river flooded every spring, the farmers built their houses on the hill.
cards.x: The because clause is an opener. After the comma comes a main clause that could stand alone.

cards.t: Hoping to find older fossils, the team dug below the clay.
cards.x: Hoping to find older fossils is an -ing phrase that opens the sentence. The main clause follows the comma.

cards.t: The bridge, which opened in 1932, still carries trains.
cards.x: The which clause is an aside between commas. Lift it out and The bridge still carries trains is left.

cards.t: Many of them were painted on silk.
cards.x: With which in place of them, this would be a fragment: many of which opens a describing clause.

cards.t: Known for its long winters, the town holds a festival every January.
cards.x: Known for its long winters is an -ed phrase describing the town. The main clause follows the comma.

cards.t: Although the test was short, it covered every unit.
cards.x: The although clause leans on the main clause after the comma, and that main clause is there.

cards.t: The researchers who studied the ice for a decade found traces of ancient dust.
cards.x: The who clause has its own verb, studied. The main clause has found: The researchers found traces of ancient dust.

cards.t: Studying the ice cores took the team nearly a decade.
cards.x: Here the -ing phrase is the subject: studying the ice cores is what took a decade. Took is a tensed verb.

cards.t: To finish the mural by spring seemed impossible.
cards.s: To finish the mural by spring
cards.x: The to phrase is the subject: finishing by spring is what seemed impossible. Seemed is a tensed verb.

cards.t: The samples collected in 2019 were stored in a freezer.
cards.x: Collected in 2019 describes the samples. The tensed verb comes after it.

cards.t: When the lights went out, the orchestra kept playing.
cards.x: The when clause is an opener, and the main clause after the comma completes it.

cards.t: Rain fell.
cards.x: Two words are enough: a subject and a tensed verb. Length has nothing to do with it.

cards.t: The museum has reopened, and its roof no longer leaks.
cards.x: Two main clauses joined by a comma and and. Either one could stand alone: its roof no longer leaks has its own subject and verb.

cards.t: Each of the two maps shows a different coastline.
cards.x: Of the two maps is a prepositional phrase, so the subject is each, and its verb is shows.

cards.t: Below the clay lay a layer of ash.
cards.x: The order is flipped: the verb comes before its subject, a layer of ash. A subject and a tensed verb still make a sentence.

cards.t: However, the second trial failed.
cards.x: However is a transition that comments on the sentence before. What follows the comma is a full clause.

cards.t: Scientists studying the ice cores from Greenland.
cards.x: Studying is an -ing form with no helping verb, so scientists never gets a tensed verb.
cards.fix: Scientists studied the ice cores from Greenland.

cards.t: The team hoping to finish the survey before the rains.
cards.x: Hoping is an -ing form and to finish a to form. Neither is a tensed verb.
cards.fix: The team hoped to finish the survey before the rains.

cards.t: A novel published in 1925 and set in a single day.
cards.x: Published and set are -ed forms describing the novel. Nothing says what the novel does or is.
cards.fix: The novel was published in 1925 and set in a single day.

cards.t: To test the paint for lead and other metals.
cards.x: A to form is never a tensed verb, and there is no subject either.
cards.fix: The lab took samples to test the paint for lead and other metals.

cards.t: The old mill, built in 1820 and still standing beside the river.
cards.x: Built and standing describe the mill, but the mill itself never gets a tensed verb.
cards.fix: The old mill, built in 1820, still stands beside the river.

cards.t: Having spent a decade on the project.
cards.x: Having spent is not tensed: having plus an -ed form. There is no subject either.
cards.fix: She had spent a decade on the project.

cards.t: The violinist, known for her fast tempos and her refusal to record.
cards.x: Everything after the violinist describes her. Known has no helping verb, so she never gets a verb.
cards.fix: The violinist was known for her fast tempos and her refusal to record.

cards.t: Researchers in the lab working late into the night.
cards.x: In the lab is a prepositional phrase and working an -ing form. Neither gives researchers a tensed verb.
cards.fix: Researchers in the lab were working late into the night.

cards.t: Two new species of frog, both found in the cloud forests of Ecuador.
cards.x: Found has no helping verb here, so it only describes the frogs. With were in front, it becomes a verb.
cards.fix: Two new species of frog were found in the cloud forests of Ecuador.

cards.t: The first printed map of the city, drawn by a sailor in 1562.
cards.x: Drawn is an -ed form describing the map. The map itself has no verb.
cards.fix: The first printed map of the city was drawn by a sailor in 1562.

cards.t: Because the river flooded the lower fields every spring.
cards.x: The river flooded is a clause, but because makes it lean on a main clause, and none follows.
cards.fix: Because the river flooded the lower fields every spring, farmers planted on the hills.

cards.t: Although the first test showed no trace of iron.
cards.x: Although sets up a contrast with a main clause that never arrives.
cards.fix: Although the first test showed no trace of iron, the second found plenty.

cards.t: When the city finally opened its new library in 1998.
cards.x: A when clause gives the time of something else, and the something else is missing.
cards.fix: When the city finally opened its new library in 1998, the old one became a museum.

cards.t: While most of the class preferred the shorter route.
cards.x: While makes the clause lean on another one. Drop it, or add the main clause it needs.
cards.fix: Most of the class preferred the shorter route.

cards.t: Since the bridge was closed for repairs all summer.
cards.x: Since gives a reason, and the result it explains never comes.
cards.fix: Since the bridge was closed for repairs all summer, the ferry ran twice as often.

cards.t: If the samples are stored above freezing for more than a day.
cards.x: An if clause is a condition, and the sentence stops before saying what happens then.
cards.fix: If the samples are stored above freezing for more than a day, they spoil.

cards.t: Even though the composer never heard the symphony performed.
cards.x: Even though works like although: the clause after it cannot stand alone.
cards.fix: The composer never heard the symphony performed.

cards.t: Unless the committee approves the budget by Friday.
cards.x: Unless brings in a condition, and the main clause it belongs to is missing.
cards.fix: Unless the committee approves the budget by Friday, the project will stop.

cards.t: Whereas earlier maps showed the river running north.
cards.x: Whereas sets up a contrast, and the other half of it never comes.
cards.fix: Whereas earlier maps showed the river running north, the new survey shows it bending east.

cards.t: Many of which were painted on silk.
cards.x: Which makes this a describing clause with nothing here to describe. Many of them would make a sentence.
cards.fix: Many of them were painted on silk.

cards.t: The bridge, which opened in 1932 after six years of work.
cards.x: The only tensed verb, opened, belongs to the which clause. The bridge itself never gets a verb.
cards.fix: The bridge opened in 1932 after six years of work.

cards.t: The researchers who studied the ice for nearly a decade.
cards.x: Studied is the verb of the who clause. The researchers need a verb of their own.
cards.fix: The researchers who studied the ice for nearly a decade found traces of ancient dust.

cards.t: Some of whom had never left their village before.
cards.x: Whom points back to people in another sentence, so this clause cannot stand alone. Some of them would make a sentence.
cards.fix: Some of them had never left their village before.

cards.t: A species of moth that feeds only on one kind of orchid.
cards.x: Feeds is the verb of the that clause describing the moth. The moth itself has no verb.
cards.fix: This species of moth feeds only on one kind of orchid.

cards.t: The letters, most of which were written in French.
cards.x: Most of which opens a describing clause, so the letters are left without a verb.
cards.fix: Most of the letters were written in French.

cards.t: An engineer whose designs shaped the city’s skyline.
cards.x: Shaped belongs to the whose clause. The engineer never gets a verb.
cards.fix: She was an engineer whose designs shaped the city’s skyline.

cards.t: Which made the results hard to repeat.
cards.x: A which clause cannot stand on its own to comment on the sentence before. This can.
cards.fix: This made the results hard to repeat.

cards.t: The mural, which the students painted over three summers.
cards.x: Painted belongs to the which clause. Lift the clause out and only The mural is left.
cards.fix: The students painted the mural over three summers.
